question: A 52-year-old male smoker (30 pack-years) is motivated to quit. He has no history of seizures or psychiatric illness. He is not pregnant. Which pharmacological agent has the highest cessation success rate and is the preferred first-line agent for him?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NRT is effective and safe, but head-to-head trials consistently show varenicline produces higher quit rates (approximately 33% vs 16% at 12 months). NRT is appropriate if varenicline is contraindicated or not tolerated.

answers.text: Varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Varenicline (a partial nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist) is the most effective single pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation. The stepped dose titration minimises nausea. This patient has no contraindications.

answers.text: Bupropion SR 150 mg once daily for 3 days, then 150 mg twice daily.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bupropion is an effective second-line agent. However, varenicline has superior efficacy in head-to-head comparisons. Bupropion is preferred when varenicline is not tolerated or when the patient has comorbid depression where bupropion would treat both.

answers.text: No pharmacotherapy is needed; brief behavioural counselling is sufficient for this patient.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Behavioural support improves outcomes but, for a 30 pack-year smoker, combining pharmacotherapy with counselling approximately doubles quit rates compared to counselling alone. Pharmacotherapy is indicated here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review tobacco cessation pharmacotherapy. Varenicline (partial nAChR agonist) has the highest single-agent efficacy. NRT and bupropion are second-line or combination options.
Excellent. Varenicline is first-line for motivated smokers without contraindications. Remember the stepped dose initiation to reduce nausea.
